Repairer
ree-PAIR-ur
n. (one who restores what is broken down; a name promised to a people who fast rightly)
From Latin reparare, to make ready again — re-, again, and parare, to prepare. In Isaiah it renders a participle of Hebrew gadar, to wall up or close a breach, the same root behind the man sought to stand in the gap.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 58 is a rebuke of religious performance. Israel fasted and bowed the head like a bulrush and complained that God had not noticed; God answers that the fast he has chosen is to loose the bands of wickedness, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, deal bread to the hungry and bring the poor that are cast out into the house. Then comes the promise, and it is a promise of a name: thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in. A breach is a gap in a city wall — the place where defence has failed and an enemy walks in. To repair it is unglamorous, heavy, outdoor work, done in the open where the damage is visible. The reward for a true fast is not a feeling but a reputation for mending what other people broke. Nehemiah did exactly this, and his account records that the people had a mind to work, which is the whole secret. Amos sees God himself taking up the trade: I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof. And Isaiah 61 promises that the people so restored shall build the old wastes and repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations. Mended men mend.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who repairs; one who mends or restores to a sound state; one who makes amends.

expand to see more

REPAIRER, n. One who repairs; one who restores to a sound state; one who makes amends.

REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction.

BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap in a wall, or in any solid body; a rupture.

RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former good state; to repair; to bring back to its former state.

DESOLATION, n. Destruction; a laying waste; a place deserted or laid waste.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 58:12 — "And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in."

Nehemiah 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Amos 9:11 — "In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:"

Isaiah 61:4 — "And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 58 is quoted as a proof text for social programmes detached from repentance, or else avoided entirely by churches that hear justice language and assume the world is speaking; the chapter is God rebuking his own people for a hollow fast.

expand to see more

The chapter is regularly enlisted for causes it never names, as though God were commissioning a political movement and the fast were a fundraiser. What God actually addresses is a congregation that kept the forms of worship while behaving like everyone else the other six days: fasting for strife and debate, exacting labour, hiding from their own flesh. The repair in view begins at home — bread to the hungry, the poor brought into the house, the naked covered — and it is commanded to a people who are told in the same chapter to call the sabbath a delight and honour God by not doing their own ways. Strip out the repentance and the sabbath and what is left is not Isaiah 58.

The reaction against that abuse has produced its own loss. Because justice language has been captured, sound churches have grown shy of the very words God uses, and the result is congregations that would rather debate the abuse than loose one heavy burden. Isaiah gives the name to those who do the work: repairer of the breach, restorer of paths to dwell in. It is a builder's name, earned outdoors, in the gap, where the wall is down. James says pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world — both halves, and neither one a substitute for the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gadar (H1443), to wall up or close a breach; perets (H6556), a breach or gap; shuv (H7725), to restore or turn back; chorbah (H2723), a waste place.

expand to see more

Hebrew gadar (H1443) — to wall up, to hedge; the participle rendered repairer.

Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach; the gap in the wall, and the name of Judah's son Pharez.

Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to turn back, to restore; behind the restorer of paths to dwell in.

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a desolation, a waste; what the repairers are sent to rebuild.

Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth or tabernacle; the fallen tabernacle of David that God himself repairs.

Usage

"“thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach” — a name given for a true fast."

"“for the people had a mind to work” — Nehemiah's whole secret."

"“close up the breaches thereof” — God taking up the trade himself."
